tip: ar triggers soft mutation, so coll (loss) becomes goll: ar goll = lost.
'Listen to' is gwrando ar, never gwrando i or am. Gwrandewais i ar gerddoriaeth means I listened to music.
gyda causes aspirate mutation, turning p to ph: pob becomes phob, as in Gyda phob dymuniad da.
The object of an inflected verb softens: tŷ becomes dŷ after Prynodd e (he bought). Hence Prynodd e dŷ newydd.
The -wch ending makes a formal or plural command: Parhewch means 'continue', spoken politely or to several people.
Welsh has no verb 'to have'. Possession is Mae gen i (there is with me): Mae gen i gydweithwyr da = I have good colleagues.
'He has' is Mae ganddo fo in the north, the conjugated form of gan: Mae ganddo fo gar newydd = he has a new car.
waeth is the irregular 'worse', from drwg, not drygach. na means 'than': waeth na heddiw = worse than today.
The -a ending gives an informal command to one person: Caria means 'carry on' to someone you know well.
The -id ending forms an impersonal past with no stated doer: Credid means 'it was believed'. Credid bod y tŷ'n hen.
Bydda i'n is the future 'I will': Bydda i'n anfon e-bost = I will send an email.
meddwl y byd o is a set phrase for 'think the world of': feddwl y byd ohoni = think the world of her.
hen goes before its noun and softens it: car becomes gar in hen gar (old car). Most adjectives instead follow the noun.
Add -ach for the comparative: pwysig becomes bwysicach (more important). na means 'than': bwysicach na gwybodaeth.
dylwn i means 'I should', the conditional for obligation: y dylwn i orffwys = that I should rest.
An adjective after a feminine noun softens: coch becomes goch in ffrog goch (red dress). Masculine nouns leave it alone.
wrth i sets up 'as' for a background action: Wrth i'r haul fachlud, trodd yr awyr = as the sun set, the sky turned.
wedi before a verb makes the perfect 'had done': wedi torri = had broken. So Roedd y car wedi torri.
Pe bai sets up an unreal 'if': Pe bai mwy o amser, byddwn i'n darllen = if there were more time, I would read.
yn hytrach na means 'rather than' before a choice: Yn hytrach na mynd allan = rather than going out.
mwyaf means 'most' and forms the superlative before the adjective: llyfr mwyaf diddorol = the most interesting book.
gwell is the irregular 'better', from da (good), never daach. llawer gwell means 'far better'.
na means 'than', but use nag before a vowel: yn gyflymach na'r bws (faster than the bus), mwy nag ugain (more than twenty).
The relative a means 'who' or 'that' and softens the verb: triniodd becomes driniodd in a driniodd (who treated).
o (of) triggers soft mutation, so defaid becomes ddefaid: llawer o ddefaid = many sheep.
oddi wrth means 'from' a person or source: oddi wrth y cyngor = from the council. Use it, not o, for senders.
Cafodd is the irregular past 'got' or 'received', from cael: Cafodd Gwenllian y swydd = Gwenllian got the job.
The article y softens a feminine noun: cath becomes y gath (the cat). Masculine nouns stay unchanged after y.
pan (when) triggers soft mutation on the verb: clywais becomes glywais in pan glywais i = when I heard.
Predicative yn softens the adjective after it: cul becomes gul, giving yn gul (narrow) and yn beryglus (dangerous).
fy triggers nasal mutation: teulu becomes nheulu in fy nheulu (my family).
newydd before a soft-mutated verb means 'have just done': Dw i newydd blannu = I have just planted.
mai (southern taw) introduces a focused clause: Dw i'n meddwl mai John sy'n iawn = I think it's John who's right.
The -wyd ending forms an impersonal past with no named doer: Diddymwyd means 'were abolished'.
Fronting for emphasis uses sy'n: Yr Wyddfa sy'n denu = it's Snowdon that attracts. The subject comes first, then sy'n.
ar conjugates for person: arna i (on me), arnat ti (on you), arno fe (on him). Say arnat ti, never ar ti.
yn ôl means both 'back', as in mynd yn ôl, and 'according to': yn ôl y dihareb = according to the proverb.
